text:
Replacing single-negative BCE is well motivated, but no sampling strategy consistently wins. [gSASRec’s 2024 extended abstract](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/939) attributes SASRec weaknesses partly to negative-sampling-induced overconfidence; its underlying method combines more negatives with calibrated gBCE. A [2024 sequential-recommendation comparison](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276), covering random, popularity, in-batch, mixed and adaptive sampling, finds dataset-dependent tradeoffs: random sampling favors head items, while popularity-based methods can balance popularity bands at some cost to aggregate accuracy. These results justify controlled comparisons, not an assumed Electronics improvement.

Popularity correction must match the actual sampler. [Sampled-softmax derivation](https://www.tensorflow.org/extras/candidate_sampling.pdf) subtracts log sampling probability or expected count from training logits; a uniform/popularity mixture therefore needs its mixture distribution, rather than popularity alone. Deterministic top-score mining does not automatically provide valid sampling probabilities. Hard negatives also risk suppressing genuinely relevant unobserved items: [UFNRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04116) addresses this using teacher-generated soft labels and consistency regularization. This is supporting older evidence, not a verified 2024–2026 breakthrough.

Practical inference for this benchmark: compare uniform multi-negative softmax, multi-negative gBCE, then a modest uniform/hard mixture with a warm-up. Mask padding, target collisions and observed training positives; treat remaining false negatives as unresolved. Tune negative count, temperature and hard fraction within the shared GPU budget, selecting exclusively by fixed four-category macro validation HR@10. Weak sampled margins are a hypothesis generator, not validation evidence.
